title: Lungs
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System; 22.2 The Lungs; 22.3; 22.7

main.t: The paired, pyramid-shaped organs of gas exchange in the chest, enclosed by the pleurae.

simpler.t: Your lungs take oxygen from the air into your blood and pass carbon dioxide out.

deeper.t: They exchange gases across about 70 square metres of very thin, highly permeable epithelium.

facts.t: They fill the thoracic cavity on either side of the mediastinum, and rest on the diaphragm.
Each connects to the trachea by its main bronchus.

simpler.t: They fill most of your chest, either side of your heart.

deeper.t: The apex is at the top; the base rests on the diaphragm. The costal surface faces the ribs.

items.name: Lobes
items.t: The right lung has three lobes; the left lung has two. Fissures separate them.

items.name: Cardiac notch
items.t: An indentation in the left lung that makes room for the heart.

items.name: Bronchopulmonary segments
items.t: Divisions of a lobe, each with its own tertiary bronchus and artery.

items.name: Alveoli
items.t: Tiny grape-like air sacs, about 200 micrometres across, with elastic walls.

items.name: Hilum
items.t: Where the nerves enter the lung root and the two layers of pleura meet.

simpler.t: Three lobes on the right, two on the left, branching down to millions of tiny air sacs.
simpler.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The number of alveoli (“millions”).

deeper.t: The right lung is shorter and wider; the left holds a smaller volume, sharing space with the heart.

facts.t: Alveolar and capillary walls together form a respiratory membrane about 0.5 micrometres thick.
Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension, so the alveoli do not collapse.
The lungs are passive in breathing: pleural fluid makes them follow the chest wall as it moves.

simpler.t: Very thin walls let gases pass quickly; a slippery film keeps the air sacs open.

items.name: Pleura
items.t: Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the chest wall. Pleural fluid lies between.

items.name: Diaphragm
items.t: Borders the lungs below; its contraction enlarges the chest and draws air in.

items.name: Pulmonary arteries
items.t: Bring deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the alveoli.

items.name: Autonomic nerves
items.t: Parasympathetic nerves constrict the airways; sympathetic nerves dilate them.

items.name: Bronchi
items.t: Connect each lung to the trachea and branch within it.

simpler.t: They sit on the diaphragm, wrapped in pleura, fed by the pulmonary arteries.

facts.t: The lung bud grows from the foregut at about week 4; most respiratory structures arise from endoderm.
By week 28 enough alveoli have matured that a premature baby can usually breathe alone.
Surfactant is usually not adequate until about the eighth month of pregnancy.
Second-hand smoke raises a non-smoker’s risk of lung cancer by up to 30 percent.

items.injury: A baby born before enough surfactant is made.
items.damaged: The alveoli, whose surface tension is too high.
items.cannotDo: Keep the alveoli open when breathing out.
items.why: Without surfactant, the alveoli collapse during expiration.

items.injury: A disease confined to one bronchopulmonary segment.
items.cannotDo: Use that segment for gas exchange.
items.why: Each segment has its own bronchus and artery, so it can be removed with little effect on its neighbours.

items.q: Explain how the lungs expand though they have no muscle to move them.
model: The diaphragm and intercostals enlarge the thoracic cavity.
Pleural fluid holds the lungs to the chest wall by surface tension.
So the lungs are pulled outwards and stretch.
Their pressure falls, and air flows in.

items.q: Compare the right and left lungs.
model: The right is shorter and wider.
The left is smaller, with a cardiac notch for the heart.

items.q: Predict what happens to a baby born at 26 weeks without treatment.
model: Its type II cells make little surfactant.
Surface tension in the alveoli stays high.
The alveoli collapse when it breathes out.
So each breath takes great effort.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The effort of breathing without surfactant (respiratory distress in premature babies).

check.stem: How many lobes does the left lung have?
check.why: The left lung has two lobes, superior and inferior; the right has three.
Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant.

options: An indentation of the left lung for the heart
A fissure of the right lung
The hilum of the left lung
check.why: It is an indentation on the left lung that allows space for the heart.
